p_question-3695.ja:
以下は、留学生がスピーチのために書いた文章である。


紅葉の異変

サリムソフィア

　私は日本の秋の景色が好きです。秋になって紅葉が始まり、緑だった葉が黄色やオレンジ、赤に変わると、とてもきれいです。秋の紅葉は、日本の四季の「変化を感じ」させてくれるものです。

　[48] ですが、先日テレビで、紅葉がピークを迎える時期が年々遅くなっているというニュースを見ました。中には、1月になってからピークを迎えたところもあるそうで、驚きました。温暖化によって平均気温が上昇していることが大きな原因だそうです。私は、夏が過ぎて気温が下がってくれば、必ず紅葉が始まると思っていました。[49] そうではありませんでした。紅葉には、条件となる気温の変化がありました。

　葉の変色が始まるのは、1日の最低気温が大体8度以下になってからです。秋になっても、最低気温が一定の気温まで下がらなければ、紅葉は [50] 。その後、さらに寒くなり、5～6度まで下がると、紅葉は一気に進みます。また、5度以下の日が続くと、最も美しい紅葉が見られるといわれています。

　紅葉に起きている異変を知り、このまま温暖化が進むと、日本の秋の景色が変わってしまう可能性もあるのではないかと思いました。もしかしたら、紅葉自体が見られなくなる日も来るかもしれません。紅葉を通して、温暖化が身近な問題であることをより強く [51] 。

The following is an essay written by an international student for a speech.


Anomalies in Autumn Foliage

Salim Sofia

I like Japan’s autumn scenery. When autumn comes and the leaves begin to change color, turning from green to yellow, orange, and red, it’s very beautiful. Autumn foliage lets us “feel the change” of Japan’s four seasons.

[48] However, the other day I saw on TV a report that the peak season for autumn leaves has been getting later year by year. I was surprised to hear that in some places the peak didn’t come until January. They said a major cause is that average temperatures are rising due to global warming. I had thought that once summer passed and the temperature dropped, the leaves would surely begin to turn. [49] That was not the case. For the foliage to change, there are specific temperature changes that serve as conditions.

Leaf color change begins when the day’s minimum temperature falls to around 8°C or lower. Even in autumn, if the minimum temperature doesn’t drop to a certain level, the foliage [50] . After that, as it gets colder and falls to about 5–6°C, the color change progresses rapidly. It is also said that when days below 5°C continue, the most beautiful foliage can be seen.

Learning about the anomalies affecting autumn leaves made me think that if global warming continues as it is, Japan’s autumn scenery might change. A day may even come when we can no longer see the foliage itself. Through the autumn leaves, I have come to [51] more strongly that global warming is an issue close to home.

p_question-3699.ja:
(1)

　自分の言葉は自分の頭の中にしかなく、相手の言葉は相手の頭の中にしかありません。抽象的な言葉の場合には、まったく同じ意味で使用していることのほうが少ないと言えでしょう。

　したがって、議論をする際には、言葉の定義づけ(注）が重要になってきます。相手がどう意味でその言葉を使用しているのか、自分と同じ意味で使用しているのかを確認することは大切なことです。これは、論理的に会話をするうえでの大前提となるものです。

（注）定義づけ：ここでは、意味を決めること

(1)

　Your words exist only in your own mind, and the other person’s words exist only in theirs. With abstract words in particular, it is fair to say that people rarely use them with exactly the same meaning.

　Therefore, when holding a discussion, the {definition} ((Note)) of terms becomes important. It is essential to check how the other person is using a given word and whether they are using it in the same sense as you are. This is a fundamental premise for having a logical conversation.

(Note) Definition: here, deciding on the meaning.

（５）

　競争や出世にはあまり関係のない、たとえばだれかを支えたり育んだり（注1）する仕事に喜びを感じる人もいるでしょう。仕事はそこそこに（注2）、趣味に生きることを楽しむ人もいるでしょう。たとえ、受験や就職、あるいは出世などの過酷な（注3）競争ゲームのただ中（注4）にあったとしても、そしてそれにある時、敗れてしまったとしても、わたしたちの人生の選択肢はそれだけではないし、「それで終わり」というわけでもありません。視点を変えれば、現代社会にはさまざまな生き方の世界が広がっているのです。

（注1）育む：育てる（注2）そこそこに：適度に（注3）過酷な：非常に厳しい（注4）ただ中：最中

（５）

　There are probably people who feel joy in work that is not very related to competition or getting ahead, such as supporting or nurturing others (Note 1). There are also people who only work to a reasonable degree (Note 2) and enjoy living for their hobbies. Even if we are in the very midst of the harsh (Note 3) competition game of entrance exams, finding employment, or getting promoted, and even if at some point we are defeated in that, the options in our lives are not limited to only those things, and it does not mean that everything is over. If we change our perspective, we can see that in modern society there is a wide world of many different ways of living.

（注1）Nurture: to raise（注2）To a reasonable degree: moderately（注3）Harsh: extremely strict or severe（注4）In the very midst: in the middle of something

p_question-3704.ja:
(1)

　ほとんどの人が、スマホやタブレット（注1）を通して、大量のSNSやネットニュース（注2）を毎日見ていることでしょう。多くの人がその膨大な情報を読むことあるいは見ることに、かなりの時間を費やして（注3）いて、ネット上の情報に追われている印象すら受けます。その結果、じっくり考える時間がどんどん少なくなっているようにも感じられます。

　また、大量の情報がネット上に流されるようになった結果、自分に都合の良い情報にしか接しない人が増えてきています。技術革新（注4）のおかげではあるのですが、SNSやネットニュースでは、その人の履歴（注5）から判断して、その人が関心を持っていると思われる情報やニュースが目につくところに流れるような工夫がされています。

　このような工夫はとても便利なことで、それによって時間が節約できたりする面は確かにあります。（中略）

　しかし、人々が見たいものだけを見て、信じている情報だけに接すると、発想が固定化してしまい、新しい進化が生まれにくくなってしまいます。また、思想的にも偏りのある考えが生まれやすくなってしまいます。

　そう考えると、この大量情報社会においては、いかに（注6）うまく情報を処理していくかがとても大事なことがわかります。また、大量情報を、一部だけ最初から抜き出して把握する（注7）のではなく、偏りがない形で、大量に処理することも必要です。

（注1）スマホやタブレット：コンピューターの機能を持った小型の電子機器類 
（注2）SNSやネットニュース：ここでは、インターネット上でやり取りされる情報やニュース 
（注3）費やす：使う 
（注4）技術革新：技術の進歩 
（注5）履歴：ここでは、インターネット上の情報の閲覧の記録 
（注6）いかに：どのように 
（注7）把握する：理解する

(1)

　Most people probably look at large amounts of social media and online news (Note 2) every day through their smartphones and tablets (Note 1). Many spend considerable time reading or viewing that vast amount of information, to the point that one even gets the impression they are being chased by information on the internet. As a result, it feels as if the time available for careful thought is steadily shrinking.

　Moreover, as huge volumes of information have come to be distributed online, the number of people who are exposed only to information that suits them is increasing. Thanks to technological innovation (Note 4), social media and online news are designed so that, based on a person’s history (Note 5), information and news deemed of interest to that person are placed where they will easily catch the eye.

　These kinds of mechanisms are very convenient, and they certainly have the aspect of saving time. (Omitted.)

　However, if people see only what they want to see and are exposed only to information they already believe, their thinking becomes fixed, and it becomes difficult for new advances to emerge. Ideologically, too, biased views are more likely to arise.

　Seen this way, in today’s mass-information society, it is clear that how (Note 6) to process information skillfully is very important. In addition, rather than grasping (Note 7) mass information by extracting only parts from the start, it is also necessary to process large amounts in a balanced, unbiased way.

(Note 1) Smartphones and tablets: small electronic devices with computer functions. 
(Note 2) Social media and online news: here, information and news exchanged on the internet. 
(Note 3) Spend: to use. 
(Note 4) Technological innovation: advances in technology. 
(Note 5) History: here, records of viewing information on the internet. 
(Note 6) How: in what way. 
(Note 7) Grasp: to understand.

p_question-3706.ja:
(2)

　勉強にしても、仕事にしても、その能率には必ず波があり、それがないようにみえても、波が小さいだけである。つまり、人間は機械のようにいつも同じ調子ではたらいてはいないから、1時間に50個の製品がつくれるから、10時間で500個がつくれる、という具合いには計算できない。従って、脳が最も快調にはたらいているときを基準にすると、たいていのときは不調ということになってしまう。

　それでも、全く無計画に勉強や仕事をするわけにもゆかないので、一応はスケジュールを立てる。その際に、快調に脳がはたらいているときの能率を基準にしてスケジュールを立てれば、そのスケジュールの通りにことが進行することは絶対にないといってもいい。その度に、自分の才能に失望していれば、失望しつづけることになる。さし迫った（注1）状態では、どうしても脳がフル回転して（注2）いるときを基準にスケジュールを組むので、たいていは不完全な形で終ってしまう。スケジュールをつくるときには、せめて中等度に脳がはたらいているときの能率を基準にする必要がある。スケジュール以上にはかどっても（注3）誰もこまる人はいない。

　そして、スケジュールにこだわるよりは、脳の変動の波をできるだけ感じとり、能率がしお悪くても悲観（注4）せずに、必ず上げ潮のとき（注5）がくることを期待すればいい。そして、上げ潮のときには自分でもおどろくほどに能率が上がるので、そのときに一気に遅れをとり戻せばいいのである。 ;

（注1）さし迫った：ここでは、時間に余裕がない 
（注2）フル回転する：ここでは、最もはたらく 
（注3）はかどる：順調に進む 
（注4）悲観する：悲しむ 
（注5）上げ潮のとき：調子が上向きになるとき

(2)

　Whether in study or in work, efficiency always has waves; even when it seems there are none, the waves are merely small. In other words, because people do not work at a constant pace like machines, you cannot calculate that if you can produce 50 items in one hour, then you can produce 500 in ten hours. Therefore, if you take the time when your brain is working at its very best as the standard, you will find that most of the time you are “underperforming.”

　Even so, we cannot proceed with study or work entirely without a plan, so we draw up a schedule for the time being. If, at that point, you base the schedule on the efficiency you have when your brain is at peak performance, you can almost say that things will never proceed according to that schedule. If you become disappointed in your own ability each time, you will keep on being disappointed. In urgent (Note 1) situations, we inevitably make schedules based on the times when the brain is running at full throttle (Note 2), so things usually end in an incomplete state. When making a schedule, you should at least base it on the efficiency you have when your brain is operating at a moderate level. If things proceed (Note 3) better than the schedule, no one will be troubled by that.

　Rather than being fixated on the schedule, you should sense the waves of fluctuation in your brain as much as possible, and even if efficiency is somewhat poor, do not be pessimistic (Note 4) and expect that an upswing (Note 5) will surely come. When the upswing comes, your efficiency will rise to a surprising degree, and at that time you can recover the delay in one go. ;

(Note 1) Urgent: here, with no time to spare. 
(Note 2) Running at full throttle: here, working at maximum. 
(Note 3) Proceed smoothly. 
(Note 4) Be pessimistic: to despair. 
(Note 5) Time of upswing: when one’s condition turns upward.

p_question-3708.ja:
(3)

　お祭りの日は町の雰囲気が一変して、ふだんひっそりとしている街並み（注2）がいきいきとしています。そんな町の様子を「祭りがある町」として撮る。神社の境内（注3）で行われるような祭りであれば、「神社」の風景として撮る。というふうに少し視点を周辺にずらしてみると単なる祭り写真ではない写真に出会えます。祭りの中から自分だけの祭りを探し出すことができるかどうか。写真を見た人から、こういう祭りの見方もあるんだねと言われるような写真が撮れたら「祭りの写真」ではなく写真として内容のあるものになると思います。

　（中略）

　「もう何年もかけて撮ってるんだけど、いい写真が撮れなくてね」とぼやく（注4）人がいますが、そういう人は頭の中で思い描いた「上手い写真」の構図（注5）から離れることができずにいて、すでにいろいろと見慣れている同じような画像を撮らされるだけだからなのです。

　ねらった被写体（注6）を自分のものにするのだと独占する強引さがないと、被写体が刺激的であるほどその場にふりまわされてしまいます。祭りなら激しい動きに、絶景（注7）なら色彩にのみこまれて被写体に撮らされているみたいになる。

　被写体に撮らされてしまうような写真は、結局その場の説明でしかない。表現としての写真は自分だけの写真を撮ることになるわけで、それはフィクションでもあるのですから、つねに「私はこう見た」「私はこう撮った」を撮るのです。

（注1）一変する：すっかり変わる 
（注2）街並み：ここでは、町の様子 
（注3）境内：ここでは、敷地内 
（注4）ぼやく：不満を言う 
（注5）構図：画面の構成 
（注6）被写体：写真に撮る対象 
（注7）絶景：素晴らしい景色

(3)

　On festival days, the atmosphere of the town is transformed, and streets that are usually quiet (Note 2) come alive. Capture such scenes as a “town with a festival.” If the festival takes place within a shrine’s precincts (Note 3), photograph it as a landscape of the “shrine.” By slightly shifting your viewpoint to the surroundings in this way, you can encounter photographs that are more than just festival snapshots. Can you discover your own personal festival within the festival? If you can take photos that make viewers say, “So this is another way to look at a festival,” then they become photographs with substantive content, rather than merely “festival photos.”

　(Omitted.)

　Some people grumble (Note 4), “I’ve been shooting for years, but I just can’t get good photos.” Such people cannot free themselves from the composition (Note 5) of the “good photo” they imagine in their heads and end up being made to take images similar to the many they’ve already grown accustomed to seeing.

　Unless you have the assertiveness to “claim” the intended subject (Note 6) as your own—to monopolize it—you will be tossed about by the scene the more stimulating the subject is. In a festival, you get swallowed by the intense movement; with a spectacular view (Note 7), you are swallowed by the colors, and it feels as if the subject is making you take the photo.

　Photos taken as if the subject compelled you are, in the end, nothing more than explanations of the scene. As photographic expression, you must take photos that are uniquely yours, and since that is also a kind of fiction, you should always photograph “this is how I saw it,” “this is how I shot it.”

(Note 1) To be transformed: to change completely. 
(Note 2) Streetscape: here, the appearance of the town. 
(Note 3) Shrine precincts: here, the grounds. 
(Note 4) Grumble: to complain. 
(Note 5) Composition: the arrangement of the frame. 
(Note 6) Subject: the object photographed. 
(Note 7) Spectacular view: a magnificent landscape.

p_question-3710.ja:
(4)
　何事もそうですが、「できる人」は応用がききます。接客が完全にマニュアル化されているファーストフード店に行っても、やはりスタッフの差は出ます。たまたま時間のかかるメニューを頼んでしまった際の事前説明、セットメニューに関する質問への対応など、ちょっと注意して観察してみると、頭の回転と表現力の差は随所（注1）に表れてきます。

（中略）

　もっと高度な判断を求められる仕事の現場はどうでしょう。どんな仕事にも、マニュアルもしくは（注2）マニュアルに類するような規準があります。その中で「できる人」は、それぞれの仕事にあるマニュアル的なものを咀嚼（注3）して状況に対応します。これがまさに「仕事力の差」につながります。

　簡単に言えば、「できる人」は勝手に自分で応用してしまうのです。それは本人にとっては良いことであり、暴走（注4）による失敗は別として、お客にとっても会社や店にとってもプラスに作用することが多いと思います。

　しかし今度は人を率いる（注5）立場になり、多くの人を育てる番になったとき、今まで意識しなかった壁に突き当たることがあります。

　自分が自然とやってきたことを、なかなかできない人がたくさんいるという事実。これを頭では理解しても、なかなか感覚でキャッチ（注6）できません。そのため部下への指導が、「マニュアルを越えたものが見えている人の世界」で行われてしまうのです。ところが指導される側は「見えていない世界」の住人ですから、うまく受け取ることができないのは当然です。

（注1）随所：いろいろなところ 
（注2）もしくは：または 
（注3）咀嚼する：十分に理解する 
（注4）暴走：ここでは、周囲の状況を考えないでやること
（注5）率いる：ここでは、指導する
（注6）キャッチする：受け取る

(4)
　As with anything, “capable people” can apply what they know flexibly. Even at fast-food restaurants where customer service is fully manualized, differences among staff still emerge. If you observe carefully—advance explanations when a customer happens to order an item that takes time, responses to questions about set menus—you will see differences in quick thinking and expressive ability appearing in many places (Note 1).

　(Omitted.)

　What about workplaces that require more advanced judgment? Every job has a manual or standards similar (Note 2) to a manual. Within that, “capable people” thoroughly digest (Note 3) the manual-like elements of each job and respond to the situation. This is precisely what leads to “differences in job competence.”

　Simply put, “capable people” go ahead and apply things on their own. For the person themselves, that is good; setting aside failures due to running out of control (Note 4), I think it often works positively for customers and for the company or store as well.

　However, when such a person moves into a position to lead (Note 5) others and it becomes their turn to develop many people, they may encounter a wall they had not previously been aware of.

　The fact is that there are many people who cannot easily do what comes naturally to you. Even if you understand this in your head, it is hard to catch (Note 6) it intuitively. As a result, guidance for subordinates ends up being given from “the world as seen by someone who can see beyond the manual.” But those being guided are residents of the “unseen world,” so it is only natural that they cannot take it in well.

(Note 1) In many places. 
(Note 2) Or: alternatively. 
(Note 3) To digest: to understand fully. 
(Note 4) Running out of control: here, acting without regard to surrounding circumstances. 
(Note 5) To lead: here, to instruct. 
(Note 6) To catch: to grasp or receive.

A


　When planning a new product, there are times when good ideas just won’t come. At such times, it is not good to assume it is because you lack talent and lose confidence. Regardless of innate ability, anyone can generate ideas through effort.

p_question-3714.ja:
読むことは、受動的な（注1）作業だと思っている人は意外に多い。（中略）読んでインプットして、書いてアウトプットする。そうではなくて、両方アウトプットなのだということが、私の持論（注2）である。

　そこにある言葉を読む。すると心には、文字以上のものが広がる。たとえば、子どものころ読んだ海外作品に、聞いたこともない料理名が出てくるということが、よくあった。クロスグリのパイだとか、ジンジャークッキーだとか。食べたことのないものを、懸命に想像して味わう。それを食べる主人公の舌を、獲得するわけである。①この行為は、受動ではなく能動（注3）である。「創る」作業である。本でしか読んだことのない食べものを、大人になってから実際に食べ、「違う」と思った経験を持つ人は、意外に多いのではないだろうか。もちろん違うのは私たちの想像なのだが、しかし自分の頭のなかで創った料理のほうが、断然（注4）おいしかった、ということは、よくある。

　本を読まない、というのは、だから、私にとって創造の放棄（注5）である。②つまらない本、相性が悪い本というのはもちろんある。しかしそこで、どこがどんなふうにつまらないのか、どう展開したらおもしろかったのか、自分のどの部分と相性が悪いのか、そんなことを考えていると、つまらない本はおもしろくなるし、相性が悪い本はいつか相性がよくなる日を待とうと思うことができる。私は、おもしろかった本よりつまらなかった本のあらすじを人に話すほうが、ずっと好きだ。どこがどんなふうにつまらなく感じたかを話すのは、そうそうそれだけ創造の余地（注6）があるからだろう。

　料理でも、絵画でも、あるいは家事の手順でも、創ることの喜びを知ってしまうと、なかなかそれから離れることができない。読むことの楽しみは、と訊かれれば（注7）、創ることの自由さだと私は答える。

（注1）受動的な：ここでは、受け取るだけの 
（注2）持論：いつも持っている考え 
（注3）能動：自ら進んで行うこと 
（注4）断然：ずっと 
（注5）～の放棄：～を捨てること 
（注6）余地：ここでは、可能性 
（注7）訊く：「聞く」と同じ

Many people, surprisingly, think that reading is a passive (Note 1) activity. (Omitted.) Read to input, write to output—that’s not how it is; my consistent view (Note 2) is that both are output.

　You read the words on the page. Then, in your mind, something beyond the letters spreads out. For example, in foreign works I read as a child, there were often names of dishes I had never heard of—blackcurrant pie, ginger cookies. I imagined and savored what I had never eaten, as hard as I could. In doing so, I acquired the protagonist’s palate. ①This act is not passive but active (Note 3). It is the work of “creating.” Many people, after becoming adults and actually eating foods they had only ever read about, have had the experience of thinking, “It’s different.” Of course, what is different is our imagination, but it is often the case that the dish we created in our own minds was by far (Note 4) more delicious.

　Therefore, not reading books is, to me, an abandonment (Note 5) of creation. ②There are, of course, boring books and books that are a poor match for us. But if you think about where and how they are boring, how they could have developed to be interesting, and which part of you is a poor match, then boring books become interesting, and you can decide to wait for the day when books that don’t suit you now will someday suit you. I much prefer telling people the synopsis of a book I found boring to telling them about one I found interesting. That is likely because there is that much room (Note 6) for creation in talking about what and how I found boring.

　Whether in cooking, painting, or even the steps of housework, once you know the joy of creating, it is hard to part from it. If asked (Note 7) what the pleasure of reading is, I would answer: the freedom to create.

(Note 1) Passive: here, only receiving. 
(Note 2) Consistent view: one’s usual belief. 
(Note 3) Active: undertaken of one’s own accord. 
(Note 4) By far: much more. 
(Note 5) Abandonment of ~: to give up ~. 
(Note 6) Room: here, possibility. 
(Note 7) To ask: same as “to hear/ask.”

→ It was found that these incidents have “shared” characteristics in their locations.  
❌ Incorrect Usage

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
はきはき — clearly, briskly, articulately

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
The student answered clearly and articulately to the questions asked.

**Explanation**  
The word **はきはき** is used to describe someone speaking clearly or acting with decisiveness. It is most commonly applied to speech, indicating that a person is articulate and speaks clearly without hesitation. In this context, "はきはきと答えた" (answered clearly) is a natural expression.

**Other Options**

① よく眠ったので、今日は頭が__はきはき__としている。  
→ I slept well, so today my head is clear.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
While "はきはき" connotes clarity, it is generally not used to describe mental states or feelings. "すっきり" would be more natural in describing how clear-headed one feels.

② ビルの屋上から、遠くの山が__はきはき__と見える。  
→ From the building's rooftop, the distant mountains are clearly visible.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"はきはき" does not apply to visibility. Instead, terms like "はっきり" (clearly) should be used when speaking about how well things can be seen.

④ ミスの原因を__はきはき__とさせるために、調査が行われた。  
→ An investigation was conducted to make the cause of the mistake clear.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"はきはき" does not apply to clarifying reasons or causes. More fitting expressions include "明確に" or "はっきりさせる" when referring to making something clear or investigating.

**Usage Note**  
"はきはき" is typically used with verbs related to speaking or acting, emphasizing clarity and decisiveness. It does not apply to states of mind, visibility, or the process of making reasons clear through investigation.

When I was a junior high school student, I appreciated classical music at the city concert hall.

**Explanation**  
The word **鑑賞** is used when enjoying or appreciating forms of art such as music, paintings, or performances. The sentence "クラシック音楽を鑑賞した" (appreciated classical music) is a common and natural usage, as **鑑賞** directly references appreciation of art forms.

opts: ゲームに夢中になっていたら、時間が着々

**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
着々（ちゃくちゃく） — steadily, step by step, progressing steadily

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
It seems that the preparations for next week's party are progressing steadily.

**Explanation**  
The word **着々** is used to describe something that is moving forward or progressing in a steady, orderly manner. "準備が着々と進んでいる" (preparations are progressing steadily) is a natural expression in Japanese, used to indicate systematic or methodical progress.

**Other Options**

① ベランダが着々と古くなって危険なので、修理することにした。  
→ The balcony is steadily getting older and becoming dangerous, so we decided to repair it.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
"着々と古くなる" is unnatural, as aging does not typically occur in a steady or systematic manner. A more suitable phrase would be "だんだん古くなる" (gradually getting older).

② ゲームに夢中になっていたら、時間が着々とたっていた。  
→ I was absorbed in the game, and time was steadily passing by.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
Time passing might seem steady, but "着々" implies deliberate progress, which doesn't fit with the unintentional passing of time. "あっという間に" (in the blink of an eye) would be more fitting.

④ 夕方になって、外は着々と涼しくなってきている。  
→ As evening approaches, outside is steadily becoming cooler.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
While temperatures can change steadily, "着々" suggests a measurable progression better suited for planned or systematic activities. "だんだん" or "徐々に" (gradually) would be more appropriate here.

**Usage Note**  
"着々" is often paired with verbs like "進む" (to progress) or "準備" (preparation), in contexts of steady and intentional progress. It is misapplied in describing natural changes or conditions not involving active, systematic steps.

questions.stem: 卓球クラブの山谷さんは大きな大会で何度も優勝しているのに「私（　　　）まだまだですよ」といつも言っている。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4: なんか is correct. It means "like" or "such as" when used in a humble or dismissive context, indicating modesty or downplaying one's abilities.

**Question Translation**  
Ms. Yamatani from the table tennis club has won numerous times in major tournaments, but she always says, "I'm still not there yet."

**Explanation**  
The sentence features Ms. Yamatani, who has achieved significant success. However, by using "なんか," she modestly downplays her abilities. This is typical in Japanese cultural contexts, where humility is valued. "なんか" fits best as it expresses humility, suggesting she's not as great as her achievements might imply. 

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1: まで**: This translates to "until" or "even," which does not convey modesty or humility. It suggests an extent or limit, inappropriate for this context.
- **Answer 2: さえ**: Meaning "even," it highlights something unexpected or typically not considered. While sometimes implying surprise, it lacks the humility needed here.
- **Answer 3: ばかり**: Meaning "only" or "just," it implies restriction or limitation, not modesty. It suggests she’s nothing but what she’s described as, which isn’t modest.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
In Japanese, using "なんか" is common for humbly downplaying or dismissing one's skills or characteristics. It reflects a distinctive aspect of Japanese communicative behavior where individuals naturally deflect praise to align with societal expectations of humility.

In an era where it is considered natural for each person to have their own mobile phone, I wonder just how many people live without a mobile phone like I do.

**Explanation**  
The sentence discusses the contemporary expectation of owning a mobile phone and questions the number of people who, like the speaker, live without one. "どれほど" is used to quantitatively question "how many" or "to what extent," which suits the speaker's wonder about the number of people who don't own a mobile phone.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1: どうも**  
  This means "somehow" or "seemingly," which doesn't fit as it describes a vague manner or feeling, not a quantity or extent.

- **Answer 3: どうしても**  
  This means "by all means" or "no matter what." It is often used to convey an absolute necessity or inevitability, which does not align with the question about quantity.

- **Answer 4: どんなに**  
  This means "no matter how" and is usually followed by an adjective or verb. It can express an extent or degree but doesn't work in this context where the focus is on a quantity (how many people).

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The key word "どれほど" is crucial here because it effectively questions the extent or quantity of people living without a mobile phone, which is the central interest of the sentence. It prompts a consideration of numbers or a range of people, aligning neatly with the rest of the sentence.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: 会ったきりだ is correct. It means "I met him just once, and (since then)..."

**Question Translation**  
I haven't seen him for a long time since I met him just once at a senior's wedding a few years ago.

**Explanation**  
The phrase "会ったきりだ" uses "きり," which implies that an event happened once and nothing else followed. It conveys the idea that the speaker only met the person once at the wedding and did not see them again afterwards. This aligns with the context of "ずっと会っていなかった" (haven't met since then).

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: 会ったばかりか suggests "not only met," which implies adding more information rather than closing off the event as singular.
- Answer 3: 会っただけに means "precisely because I met," aligning with cause/result construction, which does not fit the context of a single, past occurrence without further developments.
- Answer 4: 合ったところ suggests "met just now," indicating a recent event. However, it contradicts the timeline ("数年前" – a few years ago) and doesn't convey the long absence context.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- The pattern "～きりだ" is used to express that something happened once and has not occurred since. It's commonly applied to illustrate a situation where an expected or typical follow-up did not happen. 
- The verb "会った" (met) is the plain past form of "会う" (to meet), which accurately sets the time frame for the meeting as a completed action in the past.

It seems a dance school for children is going to open in the neighborhood. Once it opens, I'm considering having my daughter try a trial lesson.

**Explanation**  
The phrase "参加させてみようか" uses the causative form "参加させて" combined with "みようか," indicating the speaker intends to let their daughter participate or try the class. The use of "させる" (causative) shows that the action is being done by the daughter but initiated or allowed by the speaker. "みようか" suggests that this is something being considered or tried out.

1. 参加してみようか: This option means "Shall we try participating?" which suggests the speaker is considering trying the class themselves, not having the daughter try it.
3. 参加してみてよかった: This means "It was good to try participating," which indicates the action has already occurred in the past and does not fit the future consideration context.
4. 参加させてみてよかった: This translates to "It was good to have (my daughter) try participating." Similar to option 3, it suggests a past action, which isn't suitable since the text implies an action to be taken after the opening.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- "させる" is a causative verb form used to indicate making or allowing someone to do something. 
- "みる" combined with "ようか" suggests consideration or an attempt to do something.

questions.stem: （カメラ屋で）客「カメラを海に落としてしまって、電源が入らないんです。中に水が入ってしまったようなのですが…」。店員「海水が入った（　　　）、修理は難しいかもしれませんが、一応見てみますね」
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: のであれば is correct. It means "if" or "if it is the case that" in this context.

**Question Translation**  
(Customer in a camera shop)  
Customer: "I dropped my camera in the sea, and it won't turn on. It seems water has gotten inside..."  
Clerk: "If seawater has gotten inside, it might be difficult to repair, but I'll take a look anyway."

**Explanation**  
The phrase "のであれば" is used to express a condition or an assumption set by the conversation. It translates as "if" or "if it is the case that." It is often used when deducing or assuming something based on information provided. In the dialogue, the clerk is acknowledging the customer's situation and stating what follows from that condition (that repair might be difficult).

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 2: ことであれば**: This form is less common in general conditional clauses. It would mean something like "if it is the fact that," but it doesn't fit naturally in this kind of technical conditional setup.
- **Answer 3: のであって**: This form is used to explain reasons or factual conditions but emphasizes ongoing or inevitable facts rather than simple conditionality. It doesn’t fit the sense of supposition needed here.
- **Answer 4: ことであって**: Similar to answer 2, this phrase is not used for common conditional phrases and would not be appropriate in this context when trying to convey a conditional possibility.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The structure "ので" in Japanese is used to explain reasons or conditions, acting much like "because" or "if" in English, depending on the context. When paired with "あれば," it becomes a conditional form implying "if it is (the case)," making it suitable for hypothetical or conditional statements.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 少しずつやっておこう is correct. It means "Let's do it little by little."

**Question Translation**  
Mother: "There is still time until the move, but let's do things little by little to avoid panicking at the last minute. Make sure you also proceed with sorting out the luggage."  
Son: "Okay, got it."

**Explanation**  
The phrase 少しずつやっておこう (Let's do it little by little) suggests gradually preparing over time. This matches the mother's concern about not panicking as the moving date approaches and leads to the suggestion to begin relaxing and handling tasks incrementally.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1: しだけていいのに**  
  This phrase is grammatically incorrect and does not convey a coherent meaning. It seems to be an incomplete or incorrect expression not fitting the context of preparation.
  
- **Answer 2: 少しだけならよくても**  
  Translates to "Even if it's just a little." This option indicates a condition that temporarily allows something, which doesn’t align with the context of preparation and gradual execution needed in moving tasks.
  
- **Answer 4: 少しずつならよくて**  
  Translates to "If it's little by little, then it's fine." This suggests a condition where doing things little by little is acceptable, but it lacks the proactive nuance of actually starting or doing something, which the mother's statement needs.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The phrase 少しずつ (sukoshi-zutsu) means "little by little" and is a common way to express doing something gradually. The verb やっておこう (yatte-okō) comes from やる (to do) and the volitional form combined with おく (oku), indicating to prepare or take care of something in advance to prevent future issues, such as panicking before a move. This structure emphasizes proactive and gradual preparation, fitting the scenario described.

Answer (★ Position)  
Answer 2: わかる (★ is 2nd)

Correct Order  
3 → 2 → 1 → 4  
📌 ことから → わかる → ように → 春を代表する

Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown  
③ ことから — “from the fact that …”; sets the basis/reason  
② わかる — “is understood/you can tell”; forms “ことからわかる”  
① ように — “as”; with わかる makes “わかるように” = “as you can tell”  
④ 春を代表する — “representing spring”; adjective clause modifying 魚

Reconstructed Sentence  
「さわら」という魚は、漢字で「鰆」と書くことからわかるように、春を代表する魚の一つです。  
→ As you can tell from the fact that it’s written “鰆” in kanji, the fish called “sawara” is one of the fish that represent spring.

Why This Order Works  
- ことから introduces the basis (“from the fact it’s written ‘鰆’”).  
- わかるように makes an adverbial “as is evident/you can tell” clause.  
- 春を代表する then directly modifies 魚.  
- The flow naturally links the evidence to the conclusion about the fish.

④ 感めることがない — “hardly ever praises”; relative clause modifying 部長 (“a manager who rarely praises (normally)”)
② 部長が — “the manager” as the subject
③ 感める — “praises”; main verb placed in the starred third slot
① ぐらい — “to the extent that; so … that”

会議での西山さんのプレゼンは、普段はなかなか感めることがない部長が感めるぐらい、素晴らしかった。
→ Nishiyama’s presentation in the meeting was so excellent that even the manager, who normally hardly ever praises, praised it.

Why This Order Works
- The relative clause 感めることがない modifies 部長, setting up “a manager who rarely praises.”
- 感める (★) is the main action the rare-praising manager actually did this time.
- ぐらい marks the degree: “so … that (even he) praised.”

Answer (★ Position)

③ 温度や風の強さなど — “(factors like) humidity and wind strength, etc.”

Why This Order Works
1) 「同じ気温**でも**」 sets the concessive frame. 2) 「**〜など**」 lists factors. 3) 「**によって**」 links factors to variation. 4) The topic 「**感じ方**」 then takes the predicate 「大きく変わる」.

木の葉と卵を落とし、生まれた幼虫は食料をその葉で巻いて隠す。
卵を木の葉で包んで落とし、生まれた幼虫はその中でその葉を食べる
落ちている木の葉に卵を産んで包み、幼虫はその中で生まれて育つ。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 卵を木の葉で包んで落とし、生まれた幼虫はその中でその葉を食べる is correct. It means "They wrap the eggs in leaves and drop them, and the hatched larvae eat the leaves inside."

**Question Translation**  
What does the author say about the insect called Otombumi?

**Explanation**  
The passage explains that Otombumi insects create small roll-like structures using leaves to protect their larvae. The female wraps her eggs carefully in a leaf and lets it fall to the ground. The larvae hatch inside and eat the leaf from the inside as they grow. Thus, Answer 3 accurately describes this process: the egg is wrapped in a leaf, dropped, and the larvae feed on that leaf once they hatch.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: 食料を木の葉で包んで落とし、幼虫はそれを見つけて食べる ("Wrap food in a leaf and drop it; the larvae find it and eat it"). This is incorrect because it states the food is wrapped in a leaf and larvae find it, whereas the passage specifies that the egg, not food, is wrapped, and it doesn't mention the larvae needing to find it.
- Answer 2: 木の葉と卵を落とし、生まれた幼虫は食料をその葉で巻いて隠す。("Drop leaves and eggs; the born larvae use the leaves to wrap and hide the food"). Incorrect as it implies larvae wrap food themselves, which contradicts the passage mentioning that larvae eat the leaf they hatched in, not wrapping anything themselves.
- Answer 4: 落ちている木の葉に卵を産んで包み、幼虫はその中で生まれて育つ ("Lay eggs in fallen leaves and wrap them, the larvae are born and grow inside"). Incorrect as it suggests the eggs are laid in fallen leaves, whereas the passage states the eggs are wrapped before being dropped.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- [甲虫|こうちゅう] (kōchū) translates to "beetle" and refers to the insect family.
- The term 習性 (しゅうせい) is used in the passage to describe a species-specific behavior or habit.
- The verb 包む (つつむ) is an important action word here, meaning "to wrap." Understanding its role is key in identifying the process described.

1, Some people find joy in non-competitive lives: It gives examples like jobs where you support or raise someone, or people who live enjoying hobbies.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4 is correct. It means "Even if it takes time, we must process large amounts of information without bias."

**Question Translation**  
Which statement aligns with the author's opinion about the information society with large volumes of data?

**Explanation**  
The passage discusses the challenges of handling the overwhelming amount of information available on the internet. The author highlights the importance of processing information in a way that avoids bias, rather than just consuming convenient information that reinforces one's existing beliefs. This is particularly emphasized in the last paragraph, where the author states the significance of dealing with information in an unbiased manner: "偏りがない形で、大量に処理することも必要です" (processing information without bias is necessary).

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: "発想が固定化しないように、大量の情報を工夫して処理しなければならない" implies processing information in a creative way to avoid fixed ideas. The passage does not specifically state the need for creative processing to avoid fixed ideas but stresses processing without bias.

- 偏り (かたより): This word means "bias" or "inclination." Understanding this term is crucial here as it relates to the main point about the importance of processing information unbiasedly.
- 工夫 (くふう): Meaning "ingenuity" or "device," this term is mentioned regarding the design of internet systems to show personalized content, which ensures convenience but may lead to bias.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: 脳の調子がいいときを基準にしない。  
It means "Do not base it on when the brain's condition is best."

**Question Translation**  
According to the author, what should be noted when making a schedule?

**Explanation**  
The passage discusses the fluctuating efficiency of the brain and suggests that it is unrealistic to base a schedule on the times when the brain is functioning at its best. The author argues that this leads to disappointment when the ideal efficiency isn't consistently met. Instead, the passage suggests creating schedules with a more moderate expectation of brain performance. This makes Answer 1 the best fit, as it directly aligns with the advice given by the author not to base schedules on periods of optimal brain performance.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: "いつも脳が同じ調子ではたらけるようにする。" suggests trying to make the brain work at a constant level. This conflicts with the passage, which emphasizes the natural fluctuations in brain efficiency and advises not to expect consistent peak performance.
- Answer 3: "能率の変化を考えすぎない。" suggests not overthinking efficiency changes. While the passage advises against pessimism when efficiency declines, it does emphasize being aware of efficiency changes to adjust efforts accordingly, contradicting the choice to disregard changes.
- Answer 4: "能率が悪くなったときに変更できるようにしておく。" suggests being able to change the plan when efficiency drops. While flexibility is implied, the passage focuses more on setting realistic initial expectations rather than frequent adjustments.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- "能率" (のうりつ): Means "efficiency." It's a key term in this passage, referring to how well the brain functions under different conditions.  
- "快調" (かいちょう): Means "in good condition" or "smoothly functioning." Used here to describe the peak times when the brain works best.  
- "中等度" (ちゅうとうど): Means "medium degree." It is used to suggest a more realistic baseline for scheduling.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1:** 能率を上げるためには、脳の状態をコントロールするといい。 This means controlling the brain’s condition to increase efficiency, which is not discussed in the passage. The passage focuses on acknowledging natural fluctuations rather than controlling them.

- **能率 (のうりつ):** Meaning efficiency or performance. The text discusses how human efficiency is subject to fluctuations.

- Answer 2: マニュアルをよく理解し、マニュアルどおりに対応できる人。 "A person who understands the manual well and can respond according to the manual." This option implies strict adherence to the manual, which contradicts the passage's emphasis on flexible application.
- Answer 4: マニュアルがなくても、自分のやり方で状況に対応できる人。 "A person who can deal with situations in their own way even without a manual." This is incorrect because the passage emphasizes the importance of understanding and using the manual, rather than ignoring it altogether.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
There's a focus on the concept of 咀嚼 (そしゃく), meaning "to chew" or "to thoroughly understand" in the context of applying knowledge. Understanding this term is essential to recognizing the importance of comprehending and adapting the manual rather than following it blindly. The distinction between merely following a manual (Answer 2) and adapting it based on understanding (Correct Answer) is a key comprehension point highlighted in the text.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4: 自分にはできることでも、それをできない人もいることが実感できないこと. This means recognizing that there are things others might not be able to do, even though you can.

**Question Translation**  
According to the author, what problem arises when a "capable person" is training others?

**Explanation**  
The correct answer captures the essence of the challenge discussed in the passage. It highlights the issue where "capable people," who naturally apply knowledge and skills intuitively, may struggle to comprehend that not everyone possesses the same ability. This gap becomes a problem when they try to train others, as they might unconsciously operate under the assumption that what they find obvious is also obvious to others, which is not always the case.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: Suggests that the issue is explaining things freely without a manual. However, the passage focuses more on the assumption about others' capabilities rather than the method of explanation.
- Answer 2: Points to the inability to explain what they can't do. The passage does not emphasize this as the primary issue; it's more about misjudging others’ capabilities.
- Answer 3: Implies expecting others to do both what you can and can't do. This doesn't align closely with the problem described, which is specifically about failing to recognize others’ limitations, not unrealistic expectations.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The passage uses the term 咀嚼 (そしゃく) to mean "fully understand," and 暴走 (ぼうそう) to describe unintentional mistakes due to unchecked behavior. Recognizing these contexts helps understand the nuanced differences between intuitive and structured training approaches. Understanding idiomatic expressions and how they apply to behavior or mental processes is crucial in comprehension.

questions.stem: アイデアを生み出すことについて、AとBが共通して述べていることは何か。
opts: アイデアの生み出し方は、簡単に身につけることができる。
多くの情報を得ることで、アイデアを生み出しやすくなる。
特別な能力がなくても、アイデアを生み出すことができる。
発想のしかたを大きく変えなければ、アイデアは生み出せない。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 特別な能力がなくても、アイデアを生み出すことができる. It means "Even without special abilities, it is possible to come up with ideas."

**Question Translation**  
"What is the common point mentioned by both A and B about generating ideas?"

**Explanation**  
Both passages A and B emphasize that generating ideas does not solely depend on innate talent or special abilities. Passage A discusses that anyone can generate ideas with effort, as they are largely combinations of information, while Passage B reinforces that generating ideas is possible even when lacking the perception of special talent. Therefore, the correct answer highlights the shared theme that generating ideas is within reach irrespective of inherent abilities.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1**: アイデアの生み出し方は、簡単に身につけることができる. "The method of generating ideas can be acquired easily." Neither A nor B claims the process is easy; instead, they discuss effort and accumulating information.  
- **Answer 2**: 多くの情報を得ることで、アイデアを生み出しやすくなる. "By obtaining a lot of information, it becomes easier to generate ideas." While A mentions accumulating information, B focuses more on altering perspective rather than just collecting information as the key factor.  
- **Answer 4**: 発想のしかたを大きく変えなければ、アイデアは生み出せない. "Ideas cannot be generated unless the way of thinking is greatly changed." This is not something that both passages agree on. Passage B does mention changing perspective but does not treat it as an absolute necessity for generating ideas, as A focuses on a broader approach.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- **生み出す** (うみだす): To produce or generate. It’s crucial to understand this verb as it is central to the discussion about the process of idea creation.
- **特別な能力** (とくべつな のうりょく): Special abilities. Understanding this phrase is important as it contrasts with the ability to create ideas mentioned in both passages.

opts: AもBも、いろいろな分野の情報をできるだけ多く集めるといいと述べている。
AもBも、流行している商品について詳しく調べるといいと述べている。
Aは関連する分野の他社の商品の情報を集めるといいと述べ、Bは流行に逆らった考え方をするといいと述べている。
Aは関連する分野だけでなく、ほかの分野の情報も得るといいと述べ、Bは普通とは反対のことを考えるといいと述べている。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4 is correct. It means "A states that it's good to obtain information not only from related fields but also from other fields, while B states that it's good to think the opposite of what is usual."

**Question Translation**  
What advice are A and B giving regarding planning a new product?

**Explanation**  
Answer 4 accurately represents the core advice given by A and B. A emphasizes the importance of gathering information from a wide range of fields, not just those related to the product, to broaden one's perspective and foster creativity. This matches the part where A mentions, "発想の幅を広げるには、関連する分野だけでなく外の情報も頭に入れておくほうがいい." B advocates for unconventional thinking or going against the trend, which is supported by B's suggestion to consider opposite ideas to the norm, such as targeting high age groups instead of youth or simplifying many features into one.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: Focuses solely on gathering a large amount of information from various fields, which doesn’t entirely capture B’s emphasis on counterintuitive thinking.
- Answer 2: Misrepresents their advice, as both A and B specifically discuss going beyond just looking into current trends (流行). Instead, A discusses broad information gathering and B suggests unconventional thinking.
- Answer 3: Distorts A’s point by suggesting a focus on competitor products, and while B does mention going against trends, it oversimplifies B’s advice as just "逆らった考え方," ignoring the more nuanced suggestions.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- 発想の幅を広げる (はっそうのはばをひろげる): "to broaden one's ideas/thoughts" is a key phrase in A's advice.
- 逆（ぎゃく）: means "reverse" or "opposite" in B's context, encouraging thinking in unusual, non-traditional ways.
- 発想を転換 (はっそうをてんかん): "to switch/convert ideas," describing B’s strategy of thinking oppositely. 

Understanding these phrases aids in grasping the nuanced strategies A and B propose for innovative product planning.

opts: 実際に、主人公が食べていた食べものを味わってみること。

**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4 is correct. It means "to fully become the protagonist and imagine savoring something you've never eaten before."

**Question Translation**  
What does "this act" mean in the passage?

**Explanation**  
In the passage, the discussion revolves around reading being an active, creative process rather than a passive one. The author illustrates this by describing the imaginative experience of "eating" with the characters in books, picturing foods the reader has never actually tasted. "この行為" (this act) refers to actively using imagination to "become" the protagonist and "taste" what they do, illustrating how reading is an "active," rather than passive, experience. Answer 4 encapsulates this idea of creatively engaging with the text.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1**: "To actually taste the food the protagonist was eating" is incorrect because it suggests a literal action beyond imagination, missing the point that the exercise described is imaginative rather than literal.
- **Answer 2**: "Imagining eating something never eaten together with the protagonist" implies mere company, lacking the depth of immersion and embodiment of the protagonist, which the passage emphasizes.
- **Answer 3**: "Imagining what kind of food the protagonist likes" does not capture the essence of becoming the protagonist and engaging deeply with the imaginary experience of tasting, which misaligns with the thematic focus on imagination as a creative act.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
"能動" (のうどう) is highlighted as actively engaging or doing something of one's own volition. The passage contrasts "受動" (じゅどう, passive) and "能動" to underscore that reading, when paired with imagination, becomes an active, creative process. Understanding these terms is crucial for understanding the intended message of the passage.

Answer 2: 本を読むことは、自由に想像を膨らませる楽しい創造の作業だ is correct. It means "Reading books is an enjoyable creative task where you can freely expand your imagination."

**Question Translation**  
What does the author think about reading books?

**Explanation**  
The passage emphasizes the author's view that reading is not just a passive activity (受動的) but an active, creative process ("創る"作業). The author enjoys how reading allows the imagination to expand beyond what's written, highlighting the imaginative and enjoyable process as creativity takes over. The passage mentions that even "boring" books have room for creativity (創造の余地). This makes Option 2 the best fit: it captures the theme of reading as an enjoyable, creative activity where one can freely imagine and create.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1**: This option suggests that reading provides more creative joy than cooking or painting. However, the passage does not claim a comparative joy among different activities; instead, it stresses the creative aspect inherent in the act of reading.
- **Answer 3**: This implies that learning more from reading increases the joy of going forward. The passage focuses on the immediate creative freedom and enjoyment of imagination, not on learning as the primary joy.
- **Answer 4**: This suggests acquiring imagination through reading leads to freedom in creativity elsewhere. While reading might enhance creativity overall, the passage is centered on the joy of imaginative creation during the act of reading itself, not necessarily its application in other life areas.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- **能動 (のうどう)**: Describes active engagement, counter to 受動的 (じゅどうてき), which is passive. Understanding this contrast is key to interpreting the text.
- The terms 創る (つくる, to create) and 創造 (そうぞう, creation) reinforce the theme of active imagination present in reading.

"Four people are thinking about applying to a video contest. As of now, who meets the application requirements?"

From the contest notice: (1) Applicants must be **high-school age or older**; (2) One **unpublished** work per person; (3) **Green Tea division:** 20–30 seconds; **Tourism division:** 2–5 minutes.

questions.expl_ko: 정답: 1번 (鉄道の写真を撮るときに大切なこと). 근거: 음성 「『写真で何を伝えたいですか？』と尋ねるんです…1枚の写真の中に季節感や感動的な風景など何を表現したいかを意識して撮ることで全く違った写真になる」 — 촬영 시 중요한 마음가짐. 오답: 1. 정답. 2. 좋은 장소 언급 없음. 3. 즐거움이 아니라 중요점. 4. 테크닉은 「上手に撮影するテクニックはいろいろあります。けど、少しくらい下手でも構わない」 부정됨. 포인트: 「~を意識して~ことで」=~을 의식하여 ~함으로써. 자세의 본질.

questions.script_html:
テレビで工業こうぎょう[デザイナー]が話はなしています。

女：中学1年のとき、視力しりょくが悪わるくなり、眼鏡めがねが必要ひつようになりました。眼鏡屋めがねやさんに行いったのですが、気きに入いる眼鏡めがねが見みつかりませんでした。しかたなく1つ買かったんですが、自分の気きに入いらない眼鏡めがねをかけるのは耐たえられませんでした。同じころ、友達ともだちの家いえで出だされたジュースのコップがすごく綺麗きれいな形かたちで感激かんげきしました。有名ゆうめいな[デザイナー]が[デザイン]したコップだったのですが、ちょっと形かたちを変かえるだけでこんなにおしゃれになるんだと驚おどろきました。今思おもえば、[デザイン]ということに初はじめて興味きょうみを持もったのがこのころでした。

questions.translation_en:

I reluctantly bought one pair, but I couldn’t stand wearing glasses I didn’t like. Around that time, I visited a friend’s house and saw a juice cup with a beautiful shape—it moved me. It was designed by a famous designer, and I was amazed that just a small change in shape could make something so stylish. Looking back, that was when I first became interested in design.

What is the designer talking about?

2. Popular glasses designs

4. The reason she first became interested in design

questions.script_html:
ラジオで[タレント]が話はなしています。

男： [タレント]の仕事しごとを始はじめて30年ねんが経たちました。ありがたいことにいろいろな仕事しごとをいただき、充実じゅうじつした日々ひびを送おくっています。ただ、仕事しごとが多おおすぎて、時間管理じかんかんりの必要性ひつようせいを感かんじます。限かぎられた時間じかんの中でややりたい仕事しごとを全部ぜんぶはできないのだから何なにをするかの優先順位ゆうせんじゅんいをつけて、できることを確実かくじつに進すすめ、できないことは諦あきらめるということを意識いしきして生活せいかつしています。

questions.translation_en:

questions.script_html:

M: Do you like traveling? When we think of travel, some people may imagine going to faraway places. But for example, I think even getting off the train one stop early and walking home by a different route is also a kind of journey. What matters isn’t the distance, but the act of moving itself. Enjoying the different process of getting to your destination—that’s also travel, isn’t it?

2. Planning a solo trip

questions.expl_ko: 정답: 4번 (自分が考える旅というもの). 근거: 음성 「電車で1駅手前で降りて、いつもと違う道を歩いて帰るのも旅だと思うんです。距離ではなく、移動そのものが重要…そういうのも旅だと言えるのではないでしょうか」 — 자신만의 여행 정의. 오답: 1. 추억 회상 아님. 2. 혼자 여행 계획 아님. 3. 중요성보다 정의 제시. 4. 정답. 포인트: 「~と言えるのではないでしょうか」=~라고 할 수 있지 않을까요. 자신의 견해 제시.

questions.script_html:

questions.script_html:

questions.script_html:

questions.script_html:

地域ちいきのボランティアグループのリーダーとメンバー2人にんが話はなしています。

男1：僕たちが市しと協力きょうりょくして定期的ていきてきにゴミ拾ひろいをしている東ひがし公園こうえん、ゴミを置おいていっちゃう人ひとが多おおいよね。何なにか対策たいさくを考かんがえて市役所しやくしょに提案ていあんしようと思おもうんだ。
女：お菓子かしの袋ふくろとかペットボトルとか、置おいていっちゃう人ひとがいるんですよね。
男1：市しの方針ほうしんでゴミ箱ばこは置おかないことになってるからね。
男2：特にゴミが多おおいところから対策たいさくを考かんがえたほうがいいんじゃないですか？ゴミが目立めだつところに花壇かだんを作つくるとか。他の公園こうえんで花壇かだんを作つくったら、その周まわりはゴミが減へったそうですよ。
男1：ゴミが多おおいのは[ベンチ]の周まわりだよね？あそこに花壇かだんを作つくるのは難むずかしいんじゃないかな。
男2：じゃ、代かわりに[ベンチ]をもっと明あかるい色いろにして花はなの絵えも描かいたらどうですか？きれいでちゃんと手入ていれされている印象いんしょうがあるとゴミを置おいていきにくいと思おもいます。
男1：なるほど。
女：私は公園こうえん全体ぜんたいを考かんがえたほうがいいと思おもうんですが…。「ゴミを持もち帰かえりましょう」って書かいた看板かんばんを増ふやすのはどうですか？
男1：うーん、すでにいくつか立たってあるから、今以上いまいじょうに増ふやす必要ひつようないんじゃないかな？
女：あと、私たちボランティアが見回みまわって、ゴミを持もって帰かえってもらうように直接ちょくせつ声こえを掛かけるのも効果こうかがあると思おもいますけど。
男1：ボランティアの負担ふたんが大おおきくなるのはちょっとね。うーん、まず、ゴミが多おおいところからなんとかしよう。花壇かだんを作つくる代かわりにっていうアイディアが良よさそうだね。市役所しやくしょの担当者たんとうしゃに早速さっそく提案ていあんしてみよう。

公園こうえんのゴミを減へらすため、何なにを市役所しやくしょに提案ていあんすることにしましたか。
1. [ベンチ]の近ちかくに花壇かだんを作つくること
2. [ベンチ]を塗ぬり直なおしてきれいにすること
3. 看板かんばんを立たてること
4. 公園こうえんを見回みまわること

The leader and two members of a local volunteer group are talking.

M1: In the East Park where we regularly cooperate with the city to pick up garbage, there are many people who leave trash. I think we should come up with some countermeasures and propose them to the city office.
F: There are people who leave snack bags and plastic bottles, right?
M1: Yes, since the city’s policy is not to place trash cans.
M2: Maybe we should take action in areas where there’s a lot of garbage. In other parks, they built flower beds and the garbage around them decreased.
M1: The area with the most garbage is around the benches, right? It might be hard to make flower beds there.
M2: Then how about repainting the benches in brighter colors and adding flower designs? If they look well cared for, people may be less likely to leave trash.
M1: I see.
F: I think we should consider the whole park. How about putting up more signs that say “Please take your trash home”?
M1: Hmm, there are already several signs, so we might not need more.
F: Also, if we volunteers patrol the park and directly ask people to take their trash home, that might be effective.
M1: That might put too much burden on the volunteers. Hmm, let’s start by focusing on areas with a lot of trash. The idea of repainting the benches sounds good. Let’s propose it to the city office.

To reduce the amount of garbage in the park, what did they decide to propose to the city office?
1. Build flower beds near the benches
2. Repaint the benches to make them look clean
3. Put up more signs
4. Patrol the park

港みなとで行おこなわれているイベントでアナウンスを聞きいた後あと、女おんなの人ひとと男おとこの人ひとが話はなしています。

女1：本日は桜港祭さくらみなとまつりにお越こしいただき、ありがとうございます。会場かいじょうは4つに分わかれています。各会場かいじょうについてご案内あんないいたします。中央会場かいじょうでは、今朝捕とれた魚さかなや貝かいをその場ばで焼やいてお召めし上あがりいただけます。こちらは、なくなり次第しだい終了しゅうりょういたします。南会場かいじょうでは、初心者しょしんしゃ向けの釣つり教室きょうしつを開催かいさいしています。道具どうぐの貸かし出だしはもちろん、餌えさの付つけ方かたなどもお教おしえいたします。東会場かいじょうでは、海うみの生いき物ものが観察かんさつできます。地元じもとの海うみの生いき物ものを間近まぢかで見みることができ、子供こどもも大人おとなもお楽たのしみいただけます。西会場かいじょうでは、新鮮しんせんな魚介類ぎょかいるいを販売はんばいしております。ぜひお買かい求もとめください。

女2：新鮮しんせんな魚さかな、おいしそう。なくなる前まえに早はやく行いかない？
男：え？早速さっそく買かい物もの？先さきに買かっちゃうと持もって歩あるくの大変たいへんじゃない？
女2：あ、そうじゃなくて自分じぶんたちで焼やいて食たべられるって方ほう。買い物ものは最後さいごにしようよ。
男：ああ、じゃ、まずはそこに行いこう。それから近ちかくで生いき物ものを観察かんさつできるっていうのに行いかない？
女2：いいよ。釣つりは行いかないの？好すきでしょ？今日きょうもややりたいんじゃない？
男：うーん、初心者しょしんしゃ向けって言いってたから今日きょうはしなくていいかな。

質問1しつもんいち：二人ふたりは最初さいしょにどの会場かいじょうに行いきますか。
質問2しつもんに：二人ふたりは2番目ばんめにどの会場かいじょうに行いきますか。
questions.translation_en:
After hearing an announcement at an event held at the port, a man and a woman are talking.

F1: Thank you for coming to the Sakura Port Festival today. The event is divided into four venues. Let me guide you through each. At the central venue, you can enjoy freshly caught fish and shellfish grilled on the spot. This area will close once food runs out. At the south venue, there is a fishing class for beginners. We provide equipment and teach how to bait hooks. At the east venue, you can observe marine life up close—both children and adults will enjoy it. At the west venue, fresh seafood is sold. Please come and shop.

F2: The fresh fish sounds delicious. Let’s go there before it’s gone!
M: Huh? Shopping already? Wouldn’t it be hard to carry it around if we buy it first?
F2: No, not shopping — I mean the place where we can grill and eat it ourselves. Let’s shop last.
M: Oh, I see. Then let’s go there first, and after that, how about visiting the one where we can watch marine life nearby?
F2: Sure. Aren’t you going to try fishing? You like it, right? Don’t you want to do it today?
M: Well, they said it’s for beginners, so maybe not today.

Question 1: Which venue will they go to first?
Question 2: Which venue will they go to second?
